Paper_name: The impact of newly self-associated pictorial and letter-based stimuli in attention holding
Summary: This research compared the attentional impact of familiar versus newly self-associated stimuli using a matching task combined with a dot-probe task. In Study 1 (N = 28 after exclusions), the self and a stranger were represented by familiar labels, newly associated geometric shapes, or shape-label pairs. In Study 2 (N = 31), participants associated nonwords to themselves and a stranger to compare familiar and new letter-based self-associations. In the dot-probe task, responses were faster towards targets following self-associated stimuli only when familiar representations were used; in the matching task, responses were faster when confirming the correct self-associated pair. Under conditions of attentional competition, prioritisation of self-associated cues does not generalise to newly associated stimuli.
Author: Gabriela Orellana-Corrales, Christina Matschke, Ann-Katrin Wesslein
Conclusion: Familiar self-associated stimuli hold attention more efficiently than stranger-associated stimuli, but this attentional prioritisation does not generalise to newly self-associated stimuli (shapes or nonwords) under conditions of attentional competition.
